78:## The curator's role and decisions
79-
80-The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.
81-
82-Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.
83-
84-A decision is consequential if it:
85-
86-- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
87-- touches microGPT: a line of the model program, its speed or its readability;
88-- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
89-- or cannot be undone.
90-
91-It reaches the curator in one of three ways:
92-
93-1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
94-2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
95-3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.
96-
97-Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.
98-
99-- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
100-- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
101-- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it.
102-- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
103-- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
104-- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
105-- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
106-- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.
107-- Propose to the curator in words first a change to how the curator and you work together: what you say to the curator, the asks, the held list and the review list. Make it only after the curator approves.
108-- Make any other change to a skill yourself, and tell the curator when it lands: what changed, why, what it fixes, and any risk to watch for.
109-
110-## The facts of this environment
111-
112-- The curator reads on an iPhone, often while iOS Speak reads aloud at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.
113-- A repository path does not open on the phone. A page link does, and so does a pushed file's GitHub URL: `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`.
114-- The curator's client can show stale state. Answer what is in flight from the tree.
115-- The curator's time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
116-- The context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost, and a VM restart can roll the disk back. Only what is pushed survives.
117-- The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go (`fortress-repo`, its session part).
118-- The prompt cache lives an hour for the main session and a headless session, and five minutes for a subagent.
--
145:3. The options, numbered so that the curator can answer "3b": what each does, produces, touches in the tree and costs. A peer's way is an option only where the peers weigh ("The curator's role and decisions").
146-4. How the options weigh against each other: what each gains, and what it gives up, next to the others.
147-5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.
148-
149-Before you put a question, run every probe that it needs. Say whether the path to the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library, needs its answer. Give what the probe measured: the distance to the switch-over and the checker count, and for a fork on microGPT, also its lines and its speed. Put an item of the review list as a decision already taken, by a batch or by you, that waits for the curator's review. Never put it as a hold.
150-
151-Give each decision a default that the curator can take without reading the argument. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.
152-
153-**Quiet times.**
154-
155-- While the curator is away, keep your messages to the minimum: gather evidence and do the work. The curator is away:
156-  - after the curator has said that they are away or asleep;
157-  - in a turn that a check-in or a hook started, not a message of the curator's.
158-
159-  Send no running commentary, and no line that the curator cannot act on, such as a closing offer of queued questions. Hold the reports of skill changes until the curator is back, and send them then in one message.
160-- Do not tell the curator about edits to the record. When the curator asks you to record words, reply "noted".
161-- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree. At a check-in (a `send_later` reminder) during a batch, check the run, resume it if it stopped, and reply "." alone.
162-- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
163-- Send a push notification (the PushNotification tool) only for a long run's end, a hold or the model check's alarm. It reaches the phone only outside the app.
164-
165-**While the curator reads turn by turn,** hold the points. Your default, an answer to each point as it comes, buries the curator in text.
166-
167-- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of its message.
168-- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
169-- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing, so never cite a held line as the curator's yes, in the record or to the curator.
170-- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.
171-
172-**Pages.**
173-
174-- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool, never as a diff.
175-- The curator listens to a page with iOS Speak at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, which selects that section's text for Speak.
176-- Put a section's references at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points. The Select button leaves them out, so that Speak never reads citations.
177-- Give every page the house style: the CSS and the Select button's script of https://claude.ai/artifact/FoTnH7KzXt5MtGk3tTcZ8W, the plan's page.
178-- Write a page's glossary as a dictionary does: the term, then a noun phrase with no article.
179-- After a compaction, publish a page by its URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page. Rebuild a lost source from the published page.
180-

Every batch lands with the specification, the library and both paths agreeing. So the work is grouped by what has to change together, not split finer.

Two rules of the batch machinery shape the order: two rungs in one batch may not change the same declaration, and a rung cannot build on another rung of its own batch, since every rung branches from the batch's base (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:465`, batch rule 1). That is why the wrapping operators and the flattening sit in different batches, and why rung O's check follows the operators.

Fable reviews the record in place; a question goes to Pavol only where a pile-2 item needs his word. ### The verdicts

- **Rung P, exclusion over the whole parameter type on both paths: in the spirit**, with one wording beyond its brief, toward the paper. P-152 is built on both paths. The change made the two paths disagree on one pair on which they agreed before (row 787), and its skeptic found an older one (row 788) and a wrong message of the checker (row 789).

### Where the text, the brief or the principles split

**1. Rung S's reading of `extends Any` beside the specification's own `trait Tuple extends Any excludes { Object }` (fork 11, gather.2).**
- What landed: a clause each of whose types is `Any` gets `{Object}`, as an empty one does, except in `Any`'s and `Object`'s own declarations (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/desugarer/PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:59-68`, `:76`, `:123-124`).
- The text it follows: "every trait except Any and Object implicitly extends the trait Object if it does not do so explicitly" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:186-188`), said again after `Object`'s declaration (`Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:159-160`); `Any`'s immediate subtypes are tuple types, arrow types, `()` and `Object` (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:153`).
- The text it departs from: the same chapter declares `trait Tuple extends Any excludes { Object }` (`Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:180-188`), and the revival's own Appendix I says "Object extends Any alone and Tuple likewise" (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:423`). The specification's algebraic constraints declare their roots `extends Any` too: `UnaryPredicate`, `BinaryPredicate`, `UnaryOperator`, `BinaryOperator` (`Specification/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex:29-34`, `:45-50`, `:595-600`, `:611-616`). They are written so that both `Object` and `Tuple` can extend them: in the team's incomplete library, `Tuple` extends `EquivalenceRelation[\Tuple,===\]` and excludes `Object` (`Library/incomplete/basic/Fortress.Core.fsi:35-37`), and `EquivalenceRelation` reaches `BinaryPredicate`, declared `extends Any` (`Library/incomplete/advanced/Fortress.Predicates.fsi:17-18`, `:22-23`, `:42-43`). Under the rewrite, each such root becomes an `Object`, so `Tuple` would extend what it excludes.
- How the principles split. The team's text speaks both ways: its rule says `Object`; its own `Tuple` and algebraic roots use `extends Any` for a root beside `Object`. The team's code read `extends Any` as written, not as `Object`, on both paths (the base's `rewriteExtendsClause`, `:62-72` at `612869b4a`), and its 2007 test says "We ought to be able to extend the builtin type Any" (`ProjectFortress/tests/extendAny.fss:16`), which settles neither reading, since its object has its own `asString`. The live library is silent: no declaration but `Object`'s names `Any` alone. The peers split: Scala reads `trait T extends Any` as a universal trait, outside `AnyRef`, while Kotlin's `Any`, which every class extends, is the class root itself. Nothing reaches the split today: neither library declares `Tuple` or the algebraic roots (row 37).
- So fork 11's "the text settles it three times" (`CLIMB-BATCH-19.md:70`) and the record's review's "settled by the text three times" missed the text's own counter-examples. Rung S's skeptic found `Tuple` (`compile-ladder/rung-string-conversion/SKEPTIC.md:94`); the gather put it as gather.2 with no default (`PLAN.md:500`); the algebraic roots are this review's.
- **Was he told?** No. The record and its review called the fork settled; he slept from 00:48 UTC (02:48 his time) on 2026-10-20, before the batch's first result; the landing report waits for his next message, and the boot note names gather.2 among its decisions with "no default on record".

**2. Rung S's drop of `opr ||(a:FlatString, self)` from `FlatString`'s api, against climb batch 15's entry for that pair (fork 13, review.1).**
- What landed: the api states its component's header and drops the member, which the component never declared (`Library/FlatString.fsi:16-21`; `Library/FlatString.fss:34`).

Neither the record nor the rungs nor the gather named it; the merged-diff review found it and added a sentence to that entry (`25b55a1a1`).
- The principles: the library splits with itself, its api against its component; walk refuses the pair at two `self` positions, so the component cannot take it (row 726's notes; `rung-string-conversion/REPORT.md` section 10, decision 4). The text has no passage on `String`. So the component's way, the built one, wins by the library's own standard, and the fork is in the spirit. <!-- Probe P1 of the open asks of 2026-10-16: every integer power in the one library, its tests, the team's demos and microGPT, and what each contract for a negative exponent clears of the distance's six power sites, moves and costs, measured with shadow patches in a worktree at main 72a4ff655 (code as at 528438ac5), with the peers' and the commits' word. -->

# Probe P1: the integer power

Worktree `/home/user/fortress-probe-power`, branch `wip/probe-integer-power`, seeded from `/home/user/fortress-base16` (528438ac5; `main` at 72a4ff655 changes no code). Every run was niced, one JVM at a time. The worktree is left clean. The shadow patches are given inline below.

## In short

- **The six sites have three causes, not two.** On the shared library text of the error and zero contracts, the distance falls from 49 to 44. Five sites clear: `QQ`'s four and `strToFloat`'s. `strToInt`'s site keeps its exact text: "ZZ32->ZZ32 is not applicable to an argument of type Any". Its body is the `if d <- digit(…) then d radix^(n-i) else fail(…) end` of a `SUM[\ZZ32\]`, and `fail[\T\]`'s result-only `T` there takes its bound `Any`. Writing `fail[\ZZ32\]` on top of the patch takes the distance to 43, and nothing else moves. So that site needs both the power's own type and the typed `fail`.
- **Uses.**
  - Walk's suite reaches 79 distinct integer-base power sites, with 3,324 calls. All 11 sites that see a negative exponent are in three tests present since the record's first commit: `realArith`, `compoundArray` and `simpleExp`. Each writes a decimal scale as `10^(-k)`.
  - Every other value already is the integer: the natives answer it, and only the declared type says `RR64` (row 438).
  - microGPT has no integer-base power of its own. It reaches one through `strToInt` while it parses the exponents of its data (`explorations/run-c4/src/FlatData.fss:34`, `explorations/apl/mg/FlatData2.fss:37`), always at a nonnegative exponent.
- **Per contract** (the 49 are the last landed gate, `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-15b/gate/distance.txt`):

| contract | sites cleared of the six | distance | walk's 26 power tests | microGPT quick pair | library text |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| E, an error (`IntegerOverflow`; `DivisionByZero` at 0; ±1 exact) | 5, and 6 with `fail[\ZZ32\]` | 44 (43) | 23 pass; 3 team tests fail | all pass, every value line equal to the base | 15 edits, +29/−27 lines, and 11 lines of walk natives |
| Z, zero (truncated toward 0; `DivisionByZero` at 0; ±1 exact) | as E | as E (same text) | 24 pass; 2 team tests fail, and `compoundArray`'s output moves in 6 lines | as E | as E |
| R, a rational, typed by the exponent (the Working Draft's split) | 4 (`QQ`'s); `strToFloat`'s stays, now typed `QQ`; 2 new | 46 | 10 pass; 16 fail | both stop in `strToInt` | 21 edits, +91/−29 |
| X, an exponent typed so that it cannot be negative (`NN32`, `NN64`, a numeral) | 5, with the two library callers converted | 43 (with the run-to-run `LEXICO` site gone) | 10 pass; 16 fail by "Ambiguous coercion" | all pass, every value line equal to the base | 23 edits, +57/−31 |

- **The designers' later word holds a negative case.** Guy Steele's `simpleIntArith.intToIntPower` (snapshot `2eb54ef20`, 2011-11-17), bound nowhere, answers 0 for a negative exponent. Called directly, it gives 0 at a base of 2 and at a base of 0, 1 at a base of 1, and raises at every negative base, (−1)^(−1) included. So it is the zero contract with two slips (section 7).
- **Peers.**
  - Julia raises `DomainError`, except at bases ±1. For a numeral exponent it gives a float.
  - Rust types the exponent `u32`.
  - Swift has no integer power.
  - X10 has no power operator. Its `Math.pow(Int, Int)` answers a `Double`.
  - The revival's own precedent: walk refuses a negative exponent in a size (F-222).
- **History.**
  - Jan-Willem Maessen typed the interpreter's integer powers `RR64` on 2008-06-03 (c07ae816b, bfe7a5ced). They had been `Number`. At the time every integer was an `RR64` (`trait Integral extends { StandardTotalOrder[\Integral\], RR64 }`).
  - Guy Steele widened the exponent to `AnyIntegral` and wrote `QQ`'s power on 2008-07-21 (dc41d5000).
  - The revival's flat tower (d846e3644, 2026-09-27) made `RR64` a sibling of the integers, and from then on the declared type no longer holds the integer value.

## 1. Every integer `^` and its uses

**The census.** This covers the one library, the tests, the team's demos and microGPT's programs. The static types below come from reading. The run-time classes and the exponents' signs come from a census run: walk's `SystemJUTest` over all of `ProjectFortress/tests` (621 tests, one JVM, the base library), with a scratch copy of `Evaluator.java` ahead of the build on the class path. The copy logs every `^` application, in `forOpExpr` and in `mathItemApplication`, with its site, the run-time classes of both operands and their values.

The run's two failures are `ReflectTest` and `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest`, both on a `Set` `CUP` dispatch (`Library/Set.fss:124`). They pass when run alone without the instrument, and they hold no power.

### 1.1 The declarations

| where (component; api) | declaration today |
|---|---|
| `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:377`; `.fsi:283` | `opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral): T` in the component, `other:ZZ64` in the api (row 445) |
| `Integral[\I\]`, `.fss:721`; `.fsi:472` | `opr ^(self, b:AnyIntegral):RR64` (abstract) |
| `ZZ32` `.fss:799`, `:801`; `ZZ64` `:892`, `:894`; `NN64` `:975`, `:977`; `ZZ` `:1074`, `:1076`; `NN32` `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:460`, `:462`; `IntLiteral` `FortressBuiltin.fss:552`, `:554` (apis `.fsi:524-525`, `:578`, `:636`, `:674`; `FortressBuiltin.fsi:167-168`, `:213-214`) | `opr ^(self, b:AnyIntegral):RR64 = builtinPrimitive(…$Pow)` and `opr ^(self, b:IntLiteral):RR64 = self^(b.asZZ32)` |
| `QQ`, `.fss:641-646`; `.fsi:430` | `opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral):QQ`, the four sites (`other:ZZ64` in the api) |

The natives answer the base's own class for a nonnegative exponent, and `FFloat.make(1.0 / pow(base, -exp))` for a negative one (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:220-230`, `Long.java:232-242`, `NN32.java:227-237`, `UnsignedLong.java:227-237`, `BigNum.java:298-306`, `IntLiteral.java:248-256`).

A probe program under walk on the base gives:
- `2^3` = `8 : ZZ32`;
- `2^(-1)` = `0.5 : RR64`;
- `0^(-1)` = `Infinity`;
- `(-1)^(-1)` = `-1.0`;
- `2^(-1)` at `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` and `ZZ` = `0.5`.

Walk evaluates a numeral as a `ZZ32` value. In the census, a numeral base or exponent shows as `FInt`, and `IntLiteral$Pow` is reached once in the suite (`IntLiteralValue.fss:38`).

### 1.2 The one library's expression sites

| site | base : exponent (static) | the result is used as | exponent negative? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FortressLibrary.fss:645` (`QQ`'s body), twice | `ZZ` : `AnyIntegral` | an operand of `/`: `RR64 / RR64` today, the site "body has type RR64" | no: the `if -other > 0` guard, but for an unsigned exponent whose negation wraps (row 445) |
| `:4545` `strToInt`, `d radix^(n-i)` | `ZZ32` : `ZZ32` | `ZZ32`, a term of `SUM[\ZZ32\]` | no: `i <- i0:n` |
| `:4560` `strToFloat`, `10^k (…)` and `/(10^(\|frac\|))` | `IntLiteral` : `ZZ32` | `ZZ32` in `SUM[\ZZ32\]`, then a `ZZ32 / …` quotient | no |
| `Library/Format.fss:95` `number 10^(-power)`, `:97` `number / 10^(power)` | `IntLiteral` : `ZZ64` (`power`, a floor; the census reads `FLong`) | an `RR64` operand, through `IntLiteral`'s conversion | no: each branch's guard keeps it nonnegative; `:95` is reached by no test |
| `Library/Timing.fss:21`, `:23`, `:25` `w10^2`, `w10^5`, `w10^8` | `ZZ64` : numeral | compared with the `ZZ64` `duration` | no |

`Format` and `Timing` are not among the distance stage's twelve components (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh:84-86`).

### 1.3 Walk's tests (`ProjectFortress/tests`), as the census found them

- **Nonnegative exponent, used as an integer:**
  - `ComprehensionTypedBindingWalk:8` and `InferUnfixedFBoundedWalk:24`: `{ n^2 | n <- -2:2 }`, into a `Set[\ZZ32\]`.
  - `setSum:19-31`: `n^2` in `SUM[\ZZ32\]` and `BIG |||`.

## 2. The designers' word

- **The earlier word, the Working Draft.** The integers chapter declares `opr ^(self, power: NN): ZZ`: "Exponentiation of an integer to a nonnegative integer power produces an integer result" (`git show 5a68404fd:Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex`, lines 506-510).   - With ℤ a subtype of ℚ, an exponent typed ℤ picks ℚ's power, so 2^(−1) is 1/2.
  - A digits-only numeral had a natural type, `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-85`), so `x^2` picked ℤ's power.
  - The revival's chapter keeps the integer result, makes the exponent ℤ, and leaves the negative case open (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:315-320`, `:524-529`; `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3758`).
- **The later word, the team's code.**
  - The interpreter's library typed every integer power `RR64` (section 6) while every integer was an `RR64`. Its natives answer the integer for a nonnegative exponent and a float for a negative one.
  - The compiled library types `ZZ32 ^ ZZ32 : ZZ32` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:267`; Christine Flood, 489d3c1bb, 2011-09-19, through `intExp`'s cast of `Math.pow`). `NN32` and `NN64` answer their own types (`:326`, `:385`).

- **They conflict.** The earlier word gives a rational, and the later gives an integer type for every exponent. So the peers follow, in section 5.

## 3. The contracts, as shadow patches, measured

The four contracts:

- **E** raises an exception for a negative exponent when the result is not an integer. The exception is `DivisionByZero` at a base of 0 and `IntegerOverflow` otherwise. Bases ±1 give their exact power.
- **Z** gives the quotient truncated toward zero. That is 0 at |base| ≥ 2 and ±1 at the bases ±1, with `DivisionByZero` at 0.
- **R** gives a rational. Its typing follows the Working Draft: an unsigned or numeral exponent gives the base's own type, and a signed exponent gives `QQ`.
- **X** gives the exponent only unsigned and numeral types.

### 3.1 E and Z: one library text, two sets of natives

Each integer type's `^` answers its own type, on `Integral` too (`I`), in the component and in the api. The two numeral overloads change in the same way. `QQ`'s body becomes section 4's device. That is 15 edits in 4 files, 29 lines in and 27 out. Shown for `ZZ32`; the others differ only in the type and the native:

```
    opr ^(self, b:AnyIntegral):ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Int$Pow")
    opr ^(self, b:IntLiteral):ZZ32 = self^(b.asZZ32)
```

The walk natives (scratch copies ahead of the build) change one line in each `Pow` class's negative branch, and E and Z differ only in that branch's last clause. Shown for `Int$Pow`:

```
if (base == 1) return FInt.make(1); if (base == -1) return ((-exp) % 2 == 0) ? FInt.make(1) : FInt.make(-1);
if (base == 0) throw Int.divisionByZero(); throw Int.overflow();        // E
if (base == 0) throw Int.divisionByZero(); return FInt.make(0);         // Z
```

`Int.divisionByZero()` is new: 4 lines in the shape of `Int.overflow()` (`Int.java:258-261`), on the library object `DivisionByZero`.

A probe program under E gives:
- `2^(-1)`, `(-2)^(-1)`, and `2^(-1)` at `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` and `ZZ`: raise `IntegerOverflow`;
- `0^(-1)`: raises `DivisionByZero`;
- `1^(-1)` = `1 : ZZ32`;
- `(-1)^(-1)` = `-1 : ZZ32`;
- `(2/3)^(-1)` = `3/2`.

Under Z, the same calls answer `0` where E raises `IntegerOverflow`.

**Distance.** 49 → 44 on this text (947 s, `FortressLibrary` 483 s, load at start 2.32). Gone are `FortressLibrary.fss:642` three times, `:643` and `:4560`. The rest, mapped back by line through the patch, are the landed 44 site for site. The crash row stays `none`, as in the 15b gate. Adding `fail[\ZZ32\]` in `strToInt` (the base's `:4547`) gives 43 (982 s, load 2.05). It clears `:4544`, and nothing else moves.

**Walk.** The 26 tests that reach an integer power (section 1.3, with their library-path callers) pass 26 of 26 on the base library.

- Under E, 23 pass. `realArith`, `compoundArray` and `simpleExp` raise `IntegerOverflow` at their first `10^(-k)`.

- No value at a nonnegative exponent moves under either contract: the natives are unchanged there.

**microGPT.** The quick pair passes under E and under Z (`VERDICT: 7 PASS, 0 FAIL of 7`, both programs). Every value line of each equals the base run's, once the millisecond timings and parser notes are removed.

**Demos, by reading.** `BiCGSTAB`'s `er0 = 1.0 10^(-4)` raises under E and is `0.0` under Z.

**Cost.**
- **Measured:** the library text above, the 6 native lines and the helper.
- **Reading:**
  - The compiled path's checked helper for a nonnegative exponent is already planned (PLAN, phase 4, the natives; rows 523-525). Its negative branch is one line: Steele's `intToIntPower` with its two slips corrected for Z (section 7), and with a raise for E.
  - The specification gains one sentence in the entry at `basic-integers.tex:524-529`, and loses the "not yet given" of `changes.tex:3758` and of the callout at `:315-320`.
  - The three team tests above need their `10^(-k)` written `10.0^(-k)`. That is a changed line of a test the team wrote.

## 4. `QQ`'s body: the library's own way

`AnyIntegral` comprises `{ZZ, ZZ64, ZZ32, NN64, NN32}` and declares no `-` and no `<` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:441-443`). The library handles "any integer" in Fortress text with a `typecase` over the comprised types: `exactValue` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:398-408`) and `Number`'s `=` (`:386-395`). In that shape, the body splits by the sign inside each type, and negates only within a signed type, so no unsigned value is ever negated:

```
    opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral):QQ =
        typecase other of
            e: NN32 => (numerator(self))^e / (denominator(self))^e
            e: NN64 => (numerator(self))^e / (denominator(self))^e
            e: ZZ32 => if e < 0 then (denominator(self)/numerator(self))^(-(widen(e))) else (numerator(self))^e / (denominator(self))^e end
            e: ZZ64 => if e < 0 then (denominator(self)/numerator(self))^(-e) else (numerator(self))^e / (denominator(self))^e end
            e: ZZ => if e < 0 then (denominator(self)/numerator(self))^(-e) else (numerator(self))^e / (denominator(self))^e end
        end
```

- **Cost:** 8 lines for 6. The checker has no exhaustiveness check on a `typecase` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:676`, "TODO: A nonexhaustive typecase is an error"), and gives it the union of its arms, `QQ`.
- **Effect:**
  - Measured: it clears the two `-other` sites and the `if`'s test. With the integer power at its own type, it also clears "Function body has type RR64".
  - `RationalTest:699-712` passes on it under E and Z.
  - It also removes row 445's recursion for an unsigned exponent, but not the row: `XXXQQPowerExponent` still fails under E and Z, since walk's natives refuse a `ZZ` exponent (row 445, part 1).
- **The R and X form** writes the `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ` arms with `unsigned(…)` exponents, as section 3.2 needs. Under walk, that form also makes `XXXQQPowerExponent` pass.
- **Not measured, by reading:** declaring `-` and `<` on `AnyIntegral`. This adds abstract members to a comprised trait. `<` would need a heterogeneous comparison family across the five types.

## 5. The peers (P-66), from their documentation

- **Julia.** `^(x::T, p::T) where {T<:Integer} = power_by_squaring(x,p)`. For `p < 0`: "`isone(x) && return copy(x)`; `isone(-x) && return iseven(p) ? one(x) : copy(x)`", and otherwise `throw_domerr_powbysq`, "Cannot raise an integer x to a negative power -1" (`base/intfuncs.jl`, v1.11.7).
  - A numeral exponent is rewritten: "If `y` is a negative integer literal, then `Base.literal_pow` transforms the operation to `inv(x)^-y`", so `3^-1` is `0.3333333333333333`. With `p = -1`, `3^p` raises `DomainError`.
  - "If `x` and `y` are integers, the result may overflow" (`10^19 > 0` is `false`). Source: docs.julialang.org, Base, Mathematics, `^`.
  - This is close to E, with a float for a numeral exponent.
- **Rust.** `pub const fn pow(self, exp: u32) -> i32` and `pub const fn checked_pow(self, exp: u32) -> Option<i32>`, "returning `None` if overflow occurred" (doc.rust-lang.org, `primitive.i32`). The exponent's type excludes a negative value: X.
- **Swift.** The book's Advanced Operators chapter lists no exponentiation operator. Its `^` is "The bitwise XOR operator", and "arithmetic operators in Swift don't overflow by default. Overflow behavior is trapped and reported as an error" (`swiftlang/swift-book`, `TSPL.docc/LanguageGuide/AdvancedOperators.md`). So there is no integer power to compare.
- **X10.** The X10 2.1 specification (draft of 2011-02-23) lists no power operator; `^` is bitwise. `x10.lang.Math` (IBM, 2006-2016) declares `public static def pow(a:Int, b:Int) = pow(a as Double, b as Double);` and the same for `Long`, so every integer power is a `Double`. That is today's walk, and not one of the four contracts. It also declares `pow2(i:Int):Int`, commented "returns 2^(max(0,i))" (`x10.runtime/src-x10/x10/lang/Math.x10`, master; the comment was not run).
- **The revival's precedent.** F-222: walk refuses a negative exponent in a size with "a power in a size takes an exponent of 0 or above" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/EvalType.java:476`). The compiled path computes none (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/Naming.java:1212-1221`). That is a static refusal, the analogue of E for values.

## 6. Who typed the interpreter's integer power `RR64`, and when

The conversion cut parent links (`research/authorship.md`), so the commits are found by `git log --full-history -S` over `main`, and by the snapshot roots' contents.

- Up to 2008-05-08: the integer powers are top-level and answer `Number`, for example `opr ^(a:ZZ32, b:Integral):Number = builtinPrimitive("…ZZ32$Pow")` at `900bff59b^` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2705`). It is already commented so in the 2007 snapshot (`72ae6881b:ProjectFortress/FortressLibrary.fss:913`).
- 2008-05-08, Jan-Willem Maessen, dc0f919ce, "Refactored libraries to move arithmetic operators from top level into the relevant traits and objects": `opr ^(self, b:Integral):Number` on each integer type.
- **2008-06-03, Jan-Willem Maessen.** c07ae816b changes `ZZ32`'s and `IntLiteral`'s in `FortressBuiltin.fss`, in a commit about `||`. bfe7a5ced, "the last commit happened from a subdirectory and omitted FortressLibrary", changes `ZZ64`'s and `Number`'s `(* was RR64 *)` in `FortressLibrary.fss`. Both change `opr ^(self, b:Integral):Number` to `:RR64`. At both commits, `trait RR64 extends Number comprises { Float, Integral, FloatLiteral }` and `trait Integral extends { StandardTotalOrder[\Integral\], RR64 }`, so the declared `RR64` held both the integer of a nonnegative power and the float of a negative one.
- 2008-07-02, Maessen, 82c85b03a: `Integral[\I\]`, the exponent `ZZ64`, and `Integral`'s `opr ^(self, b:ZZ64):RR64`. 2008-07-10, Christine Flood, 25acd32f7: `ZZ`'s, `opr ^(self, b:ZZ64):RR64`.
- 2008-07-21, Guy Steele, dc41d5000: the exponent becomes `AnyIntegral`; `NN32` and `NN64` are added with `:RR64`; `QQ` is added, with today's body (`FortressLibrary.fss:641-646`). The tower is then `QQ extends RR64` and `AnyIntegral extends { QQ }`. It is the same at the team's last commit (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fss:422`, `:609`).
- 2026-09-27, the revival, d846e3644, "The one library's number types are siblings under Number". From here `RR64` excludes the integers, so the declared type no longer holds the value that the natives answer (row 438). 2026-10-02, 9d2e4c856, added the numeral overloads at `:RR64`.
- The compiled side:
  - `ZZ32 ^ ZZ32 : ZZ32`: Christine Flood, 489d3c1bb, 2011-09-19.
  - `NN32`'s: first in the snapshot 25f7cf913 (Jean-Baptiste Tristan, "Implementation of NN32", 2011-11-23).
  - `NN64`'s: first in the snapshot fb6bf98e4 (2012-01-05).
  - `intToIntPower`: first in the snapshot 2eb54ef20 (Guy Steele, 2011-11-17). The snapshot of 2011-11-14 (796b6d3da) lacks it.

## 7. Defects and findings, with the ledger rows they need

1. **New row (checker; the compiled path only, since walk has no static types).**
   - The site: `strToInt`'s `SUM[\ZZ32\][ i <- i0:n] if d <- digit(s[i], radix) then d radix^(n-i) else fail("…") end` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4544-4548`) is refused with the body typed `Any`. `fail[\T\]`'s result-only `T` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:37`) takes its bound in the `else` of an `if` with a generator clause, inside a reduction's body.
   - The evidence: on the E/Z text the site keeps its exact message; with `fail[\ZZ32\]` it clears (44 → 43), and nothing else moves.
   - Siblings: row 560 (fixed, four other contexts) and row 438. Reproducer: none yet (a compiled test in this shape, beside `InferResultOnlyIfWithoutElse`). The site needs both this repair and the power's own type.
2. **A note to row 523, or to row 441 (the compiled run time; unbound code).** Steele's `intToIntPower` (`simpleIntArith.java:380-398`), called directly:
   - `(2,-1)` → 0, `(0,-1)` → 0, `(1,-1)` → 1;
   - `(-1,-1)`, `(-1,-2)` and `(-2,-1)` raise. Its `Utility.makeFortressException("…DivisionByZero")` fails outside a compiled run as `FortressImplementationError`.
   - So it answers 0 where 1/0 has no value, and raises at every negative base. By reading, `a < 0` stands where `a == 0` would give the zero contract.
   - Binding it as it stands would decide row 441 as Z with these two slips.
3. **A note to row 445.** Measured under R: a `ZZ` exponent passed to `QQ`'s power from `FortressBuiltin` is refused, "not applicable to an argument of type (QQ, ZZ)". The api's `other:ZZ64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:430`) is what that component sees. Under walk, the unsigned-exponent body of sections 3.2 and 4 makes `XXXQQPowerExponent` pass.
4. **Not new, met on the way.**
   - Walk evaluates a numeral as a `ZZ32` value, so an `IntLiteral`-typed exponent overload is never chosen under walk. This is P-76's Q-walk, and it decides R's and X's walk costs.
   - Walk's abstract-method check takes no body above the abstract parameter type (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/interpreter.md`, "What walk checks"), so a narrower ring power costs a body on each ring object.

## 8. Decisions

- **E's exceptions.** I chose `IntegerOverflow` for a result that no integer type holds, after the revival's sentence "a result that the type cannot hold throws an IntegerOverflow" (`basic-integers.tex:567-568`) and P-73. At a base of 0 I chose `DivisionByZero`, as `intToIntPower` raises it. Bases ±1 give their exact power, as in Julia.
  - The alternatives: refuse every negative exponent, as F-222 does for sizes; `CastError`, the Working Draft's check exception, which is checked; or a new exception.
  - No walk test catches a power's exception, so the choice moves no measured value.
- **Z's meaning.** Truncation toward zero: the compiled `intExp` today and `intToIntPower`'s intent. The alternative is floor division, which gives −1 at (−2)^(−1).
- **R's shape.** The result is typed by the exponent, as in the Working Draft, with a numeral exponent read as natural. The alternatives, by reading:
  - every integer power a `QQ`, which drops the premise;
  - a `QQ` value under an integer type, which is unsound and impossible to compile.
- **The ring's power, for R and X.** The only way the measurement found: `MultiplicativeRing`'s power takes `NN64`. With `AnyIntegral` there, R breaks the ring's return type, and X breaks walk's load check on the integer objects.
- **One distance run for E and Z.** The checker reads only the library text, which is identical for both, and the walk natives differ only (`fortress-repo` skill: reuse a result unless the code changes). Instead, the diagnostic `fail[\ZZ32\]` run was added.
- **The test set.** The 26 tests that the census showed reaching an integer power, or calling `strToInt`, `strToFloat`, `Format` or `Timing`. I did not run the whole suite.
- **microGPT.** Each quick program was run alone, not as `mg-run.sh` runs the pair at once, to keep one JVM at a time.

## 9. For FACTS

- **The power holds five of the distance's sites.** The integer power's declared `RR64` holds five of the 49: `QQ`'s four and `strToFloat`'s. `strToInt`'s site clears only with that repair and a typed `fail` together. It means the ask frees 5 sites, and 6 with the new row's repair. The command: `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh` on section 3.1's text gives `#total 44`, and with `fail[\ZZ32\]` in `strToInt`, `#total 43`. Detail: sections 3.1 and 7.
- **No nonnegative power's walk value depends on the declared type.** The natives already answer the integer (row 438). Under E and Z, 23 and 24 of the 26 power tests pass, and every failure and every moved value is at a negative exponent. Detail: section 3.1.
- **The negative-exponent values are in three team tests.** Every walk value that a negative-exponent contract can move is in `realArith`, `compoundArray` and `simpleExp`, which write a decimal scale as `10^(-k)`. The demos `BiCGSTAB` and `BiCGSTAB2` do the same, by reading. Detail: section 1.3.
- **microGPT's only integer power is `strToInt`'s.** It is reached from `FlatData.fss:34` and `FlatData2.fss:37`, at nonnegative exponents. Under R, both quick programs stop there. Detail: sections 1.6 and 3.2.

## 10. Commands worked out

- **The power census.** A scratch copy of `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java`, which appends one line per `^` application to the file that `FORTRESS_POW_CENSUS` names, compiled with `javac -cp "$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)"` and put ahead of the build on the class path of a `SystemJUTest` run (harness-one.sh's `java` line, with `-Dtests` set to a folder).
- **Shadow natives.** Whole copies of the six glue files, compiled into a scratch folder and put ahead of the build on the class path, for both walk and the harness. No `ant` build.
- **microGPT's quick pair one program at a time.** `mg-run.sh`'s per-program commands, run in sequence, with the class path built as `bin/fortress` builds it.
- **Mapping a distance run's sites back.** Each site's line, mapped to the base's through the hunks of `git diff -U0`, then compared with `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv` by kind, place and message (span ends and fresh-name numbers dropped).

## 11. For the curator: a decision not taken

What an integer raised to a negative power gives, with the integer result for a nonnegative exponent as its premise: E, Z, R or X as above, each with its sites, values and cost in section 3. Inside the ask, but not taken here:

- E's exceptions (section 8).
- Whether the new `strToInt` row's repair, a typed `fail` or the checker's expected type, goes with the answer.
- For R and X: the ring's natural power, and that Q-walk comes first.

Written on `main` at `3f463d3b5`; it measures one thing (section 8) and cites the rest. -->

# The Fable judgement on item 58: can a combination rebuild the tower's power?

**Answer in five lines.** No, not whole. An unsigned exponent and a float or rational base are rebuilt already, by the declarations the library has. A signed computed exponent can be rebuilt by type, as contract R, at R's cost; it rebuilds the Working Draft's rule, which the team's own code and tests never followed, so the premise he took excludes it. A numeral exponent cannot be rebuilt: a numeral's sign never reaches a type on either path, and under walk a numeral has no type of its own until Q-walk, so no overload can split `10^16` from `10^(-16)`. That is the only case the team's tests reach at a negative exponent, so the hole is where the tests are.

**Recommendation and default.** E, as PLAN item 58's default: the integer's own type at every exponent, `IntegerOverflow` where the result is not an integer, `DivisionByZero` at a base of 0, ±1 exact; a float or rational base for a fraction, as the library already does; `fail[\ZZ32\]` in `strToInt`; the three team tests and the two demos written with a float base. It is itself the combination he is looking for, split on the other operand: the base's type says whether a negative exponent has a value, and the sign of the exponent, a value, is tested at run time, as the library tests every such subset (P-80). He can take it without reading on. Nothing in it reverses a decision on record.

Short names: REPORT is `explorations/perf-probes/integer-power/REPORT.md`; the review is `explorations/reviews/integer-power-negative-exponent.md`; the digest is `explorations/reviews/digest-2026-10-19.md`; B.2 is section B.2 of `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-10-19-haiku/fable-judgement.md`; `P-` is a POSITIONS entry, `F-` a FACTS entry, "row" a gap-ledger row; a bare `fss:N` is `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `fsi:N` its api; `Builtin.fss:N` is `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`; the Working Draft is `Specification-1.0-frozen/`.

## 0. Words, for a reader who knows Swift and the JVM

- `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` are `Int32` and `Int64`; `NN32`, `NN64` are `UInt32` and `UInt64`; `ZZ` is a `BigInteger`; `QQ` is an exact fraction of two `ZZ`; `RR64` is a `Double`; `IntLiteral` is the type of a numeral such as `16` before it converts into one of them (F-79; `Builtin.fss:484`).
- **Flat.** None of these is a subtype of another, as Swift's integer types are not. Each wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one, and the conversion is applied for you, but only when no declaration fits the argument as it is (P-74; F-131; `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:474-478`). `Number` is above them all and has no operators of its own (P-43; `fss:380-396`).
- **The tower** is the Working Draft's design, where ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ were subtypes (section 2).
- **Overloading** chooses, among the declarations of one name, the most specific that applies to the arguments. Fortress does this at run time by the arguments' run-time types, as Julia does, besides the checker's static choice (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:298-310`; the `fortress-repo` skill, "Dispatch is on every argument, at run time"). A declaration is chosen by types, never by values.
- **A numeral** has one type on the compiled path, `IntLiteral`, whatever its value (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:468-469`). Under walk it is an `Int`, a `ZZ32` value (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:1635-1637`; `.../evaluator/values/FIntLiteral.java:40-50`; F-74). **Q-walk** is the step that gives walk's numeral the type `IntLiteral`; it waits for the switch-over and is not designed (P-76; `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md:86`; digest, section 5, item 3).
- **The distance** is the count of the compiled checker's errors over the interpreter's library, 34 today, six of them at integer powers (digest, sections 1 and 2; F-241). **The quick pair** is microGPT's walk check, two programs, 7 checks each (the review, "Words used here").
- **E, Z, R, X** are the four contracts of the ask: an error, zero, a rational typed by the exponent, an exponent typed so that it cannot be negative (REPORT, section 3).

## 1. His question, and the three facts the coordinator gave him

His words, as the coordinator cleaned them (the brief holds the raw text):

> I need more context to make an informed decision. This seems like a consequence of flattening the numeric tower, and much of the existing library design depends on this tower. None of the options seem to fit, because it's not a one-size-fits-all kind of solution that can cover all cases. I feel we likely need a combination of several options to rebuild the original behavior of the numeric tower, but at the same time I worry that might not be possible in the current design. I would like Fable to weigh in on this. Can't we somehow use clever overloads to split the negative exponents away from the positive ones? But I guess there's no way to attempt a coercion to NN when the exponents are already ZZ… Before asking Fable: do you see where I am going with this? Is that an unreasonable direction?

The direction is reasonable, and it is the right instinct: split by type. The answer below says which types can carry the split in the flat design (the base's type, and for the exponent only an unsigned width) and which cannot (the sign of a `ZZ32`, and the sign of a numeral). The three facts the coordinator told him are checked:

1. **Overloading picks by the arguments' types, never by their values, on both paths.** Confirmed. The specification dispatches "the declarations that are applicable to that call at run time" by the arguments' dynamic types (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:298-310`); walk dispatches on run-time classes (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/interpreter.md`, "How walk evaluates a program"); the checker on static types. The one place the Working Draft put a value into a type was the numeral: `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`, with the value `v` a static parameter (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-85`). The revival's `IntLiteral` carries none (P-76; `Misc.scala:468-469`).
2. **Nothing converts a `ZZ32` into an `NN32` implicitly.** Confirmed, and stronger than stated. `NN32` declares one coercion, from `IntLiteral` (`Builtin.fss:386`); `NN64` from `NN32` and `IntLiteral` (`fss:911-912`). The explicit conversion, `unsigned(self): NN32` on `ZZ32` (`fss:806`), reinterprets the bits: `unsigned(-1)` is `4294967295`, measured (section 8). And since a coercion is chosen by type, like an overload (`conversions-coercions.tex:474-478`), a declared `ZZ32` to `NN32` coercion could not refuse a negative value either: it would convert it as `unsigned` does. So "attempt a coercion to NN" cannot be a sign test, as he guessed.

## 5. The least bad mix, and how it weighs

The mix: E's contract for an integer base (section 4.7's two exceptions, inside the run-time sign test of section 4.4), the float and rational bases for a fraction (section 4.2), `fail[\ZZ32\]` in `strToInt` (row 747), and the three team tests and two demos written with a float base. It is PLAN item 58's default, word for word. By the three principles:

1. **The team's later word** (P-26) gives the type: an integer `^` has the integer's type at a signed exponent (section 2.3), so R is out; a numeral's type is `IntLiteral` (P-76), so case 3 cannot split; the tower is flat (P-43), so no `QQ` result flows into float code. It is silent on the value (B.2).
2. **The library as the team wrote it** gives the value's shape: it tests a sign inside a body by comparison (`fss:642`; P-80), raises `IntegerOverflow` for a result the width cannot hold (`PowChooseLcmRungE.fss:58`; P-73), and gives a fraction from a float or rational base (`Builtin.fss:160`; `fss:641`). The one thing E changes in the library's own behaviour is the float that the natives answer today at a negative exponent (REPORT, section 1.1), which the flat tower already made untypable (row 438) and which no contract keeps.
3. **The peers**, where the first two are silent, between an error and a zero: Julia, Java's `BigInteger.pow` and Haskell's `^` raise; Rust types the exponent unsigned; X10 answers a float; none answers 0 (the review, section 4). The revival's own precedent refuses a negative exponent in a size (F-222).

Against the others: Z moves six printed values of a team test without a sign and is "what the compiled cast happens to do" (B.2); R and X wait for Q-walk, which is not designed, while their sites are needed before the switch-over (the review, section 6, item 4; digest, section 5), and X's conversion hides a sign error as an overflow (section 4.1). F2 buys nothing under E and reverses P-76 in part; F3 is X at a higher price.

What the mix gives up, said plainly: `2^(-1)` has no value when `2` is an integer. The program that wants 1/2 writes `2.0^(-1)` or a rational base, as microGPT does.

## 6. The recommendation and the default

E, as PLAN item 58's default and B.2's: each integer type's `^` answers its own type, on `Integral` too, in the component and the api; a negative exponent raises `IntegerOverflow` where the result is not an integer, `DivisionByZero` at a base of 0, and the bases ±1 give their exact power; `QQ`'s body takes the `typecase` of REPORT section 4; `fail[\ZZ32\]` in `strToInt`; `realArith`, `compoundArray`, `simpleExp`, `BiCGSTAB` and `BiCGSTAB2` write their scale with a float base. Cost: 15 library edits, 29 lines in and 27 out, 11 lines of walk natives, one line in the compiled helper of phase 4, one sentence in the specification; sites 34 to about 28; the quick pair passes with every value line equal; 23 of 26 walk tests pass, the other three after their respelling; no wait on Q-walk (REPORT, section 3.1; the review, sections 5.1 and 7).

**The default he can take without reading the argument:** E, as PLAN item 58 states it.

## 7. What it needs from him

- **E itself** reverses nothing on record. It carries three choices the ask left inside it (PLAN item 58; REPORT, section 11): E's exceptions, `IntegerOverflow` and `DivisionByZero` with ±1 exact, against refusing every negative exponent as F-222 does for sizes; row 747's `fail[\ZZ32\]` in the same rung; and a changed line in each of three team tests and two demos, a point to report (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/records.md`, "What every report holds"). Each has its default in PLAN item 58.
- **If he wants case 3 rebuilt**, the numeral's sign in its type (F2): it reverses P-76 in part and waits for Q-walk. My answer is no, since under E it buys nothing a program can see.
- **If he wants X**: it waits for Q-walk, removes the compiled `ZZ32 ^ ZZ32` and three compiled tests, and needs a checked conversion that the library lacks, or `unsigned`'s reinterpretation stands in every converted caller. It reverses nothing, but F3's form of it reads P-80 anew and takes P-62's work early.
- **If he wants R**: it sets aside the premise he took under P-26, the compiled prelude's integer type at a signed exponent, for the Working Draft's earlier text, and waits for Q-walk.
- **Nothing here touches P-43, P-62, P-74 or P-80** unless he chooses F2 or F3.

## 8. What I measured

One thing, since no way above changes the probe's measured text: what walk's `unsigned` does to a negative exponent, which prices X's conversion (section 4.1) and fact 2 (section 1). The probe `ProbeUnsignedPower.fss`, in the scratchpad, run under `nice -n 19` with the skill's setup lines on `main` at `3f463d3b5`, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, one JVM:

```
unsigned(-1) = 4294967295
unsigned(-1) > unsigned(0) = true
2^unsigned(-1) overflows = true
2^(-1) today = 0.5
```

The third line is `overflows(fn () => two^u)` with `two: ZZ32 = 2` and `u = unsigned(m1)`, `m1: ZZ32 = -1`, in the shape of `PowChooseLcmRungE.fss:6-12`. The fourth is on record already (REPORT, section 1.1). The native is `ZZ32$ToNN32`, `f(int x) { return x; }` into `FNN32.make` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/ZZ32.java:54-60`, `:213-216`).

## 9. For the record

- **For FACTS, 1.** `unsigned` reinterprets the bits under walk: `unsigned(-1)` is `4294967295`, and `2^unsigned(-1)` raises `IntegerOverflow`. It means that converting a signed exponent for an unsigned power, as X does in every caller, turns a negative value into an overflow at run time, not a sign error. No test checks it; the command and output are in section 8.
- **For FACTS, 2.** A numeral's sign does not reach its type on either path: the checker types every `IntLiteralExpr` `IntLiteral` (`Misc.scala:468-469`), the compiled path folds `prefix -` on a literal into a literal of that type before the checker and does not fold `^` (`IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:58-107`, `:152-153`; `PhaseOrder.java:137-146`), the numeral itself has no sign (`Specification/basic/lexical-structure.tex:1053-1080`), and walk's numeral is an `Int` (F-74). It means that no overload on a numeral exponent's type can split `10^16` from `10^(-16)`. By reading; the lines cited show it.
- **The INDEX line owed** for this note, not written since the brief allows one file: `` - `explorations/reviews/integer-power-fable-judgement.md`: `` followed by the first sentence of this file's header comment.
- **Decisions taken here.** (1) The Working Draft's `-16` is read as the prefix operator on a numeral, a ℤ, because a numeral has no sign (`lexical-structure.tex:1053-1080`) and the Working Draft gives no literal type for a negated numeral; the alternative, that `Literal[\v\]` (`literals.tex:85`) covered negative values, has no text behind it. (2) `Number` as a result type is rejected by reading, not by measurement, since `Number` declares no operators (`fss:380-396`). (3) No new combination was measured, since the least bad mix is the probe's E text unchanged.
- **Commands worked out.** None beyond the skill's.
- **Commit:** nothing, as the brief says.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:85
- P-153 **An integer raised to a negative power raises an error; a fraction comes from a float or rational base (contract E, item 58).** Each integer type's `^` answers its own type at every exponent: a negative exponent raises `IntegerOverflow` where the result is no integer, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code types an integer power by its integer at a signed exponent (P-26); overloads choose by type, and no type carries an exponent's or a numeral's sign, so the split is on the base, with the sign tested at run time as the library tests every sign-refined subset (P-80). Still to build: the integer powers so typed, with row 747's typed `fail` in `strToInt`, and the team tests `realArith`, `compoundArray` and `simpleExp` and two demos written with a float base (PLAN item 58).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:39
- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size left unknown is an error only where it is used.** The checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140). Storage refuses a JVM array length over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. How the checker represents it is not his choice. A size that a call cannot fix refuses the call, also inside an overload set, instead of dropping the arm (row 400, its compiled half open). Every static argument but an operator counts in the exclusion rule; booleans join once the checker has boolean parameters (row 406). A size used as a value converts to `ZZ32` as a numeral does (row 485). The unused sizes of the api's 17 vector and matrix operators go by decision E's diff, which he read and took for the switch-over (ask 3, 2026-10-20; `perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`): it finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which took them out of the component only (F-35), and is built with the array sites' other fixes. The other unused sizes of the 25 go only by a diff shown to him.

Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side.

- P-26 **The type group's late positions outweigh the specification's early text where they conflict.** The early text was a wish. The type group then made the language run, for performance and with specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. So their later word wins: the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiler prelude's tower flattened in 2009 and 2010 (P-43), Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper. QQ_OLD = """    opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral):QQ =
        if -other > 0 then   (* Way too clever by half (to avoid infinite recursion on 2^(-63)) *)
            (denominator(self)/numerator(self))^(-other)
        else
            (numerator(self))^other / (denominator(self))^other
        end
"""
# EZ: the exponent's sign split inside each of AnyIntegral's comprised types (exactValue's device).
QQ_EZ = """    opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral):QQ =
        typecase other of
            e: NN32 => (numerator(self))^e / (denominator(self))^e
            e: NN64 => (numerator(self))^e / (denominator(self))^e
            e: ZZ32 => if e < 0 then (denominator(self)/numerator(self))^(-(widen(e))) else (numerator(self))^e / (denominator(self))^e end
            e: ZZ64 => if e < 0 then (denominator(self)/numerator(self))^(-e) else (numerator(self))^e / (denominator(self))^e end
            e: ZZ => if e < 0 then (denominator(self)/numerator(self))^(-e) else (numerator(self))^e / (denominator(self))^e end
        end
"""
# R and X: the same split, every integer power at an unsigned exponent.
QQ_RX = """    opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral):QQ =
        typecase other of
            e: NN32 => (numerator(self))^e / (denominator(self))^e
            e: NN64 => (numerator(self))^e / (denominator(self))^e

    opr ^(self, b:IntLiteral):RR64 = self^(b.asZZ32)' % (P, n),

", "    opr BITNOT(self):NN64

", "    opr BITNOT(self):ZZ32

" + signedApi())
    e(FLI, "    opr BITNOT(self):ZZ64
    opr ^(self, b:IntLiteral):RR64
", "    opr BITNOT(self):ZZ64
    opr ^(self, b:NN64):ZZ64
    opr ^(self, b:NN32):ZZ64
    opr ^(self, b:IntLiteral):ZZ64
" + signedApi())
    e(FLI, "    opr /(self,other:ZZ):QQ
    opr ^(self, b:IntLiteral):RR64
", "    opr /(self,other:ZZ):QQ
    opr ^(self, b:NN64):ZZ

" + signedApi())
    e(FBI, "    opr BITNOT(self):NN32

", "    opr BITNOT(self):NN32

" + signedApi())
    e(FBI, "    opr ^(self, b:AnyIntegral):RR64
    opr ^(self, b: IntLiteral): RR64
", "    opr ^(self, b:NN64):IntLiteral
    opr ^(self, b:NN32):IntLiteral
    opr ^(self, b: IntLiteral): IntLiteral
" + signedApi())
    e(FL, QQ_OLD, QQ_RX)
    # walk's abstract-method check takes a body only at or below the ring's NN64 exponent, so each

    e(FB, "    (** Shouldn't need this extra declaration. **)

    opr ^(self, b:NN64):RR64 =

", "FloatLiteral$AsFloat")
    opr ^(self, b:NN64):RR64 = (asFloat(self))^b
")
    e(FB, "    opr ^(self, b:AnyIntegral):RR32 = narrow((asFloat(self))^b)
", "    opr ^(self, b:AnyIntegral):RR32 = narrow((asFloat(self))^b)
    opr ^(self, b:NN64):RR32 = narrow((asFloat(self))^b)
")
    e(FL, "    opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral):QQ =
        typecase other of", "    opr ^(self, other:NN64):QQ = (numerator(self))^other / (denominator(self))^other
    opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral):QQ =

    if C == 'X':

        e(FL, "d radix^(n-i)", "d radix^(unsigned(n-i))")

              "10^(unsigned(k)) (both[|both| - 1 - k].codePoint - '0'.codePoint))/(10^(unsigned(|frac|))))")
else:

texts = {}
for (f, old, new) in edits:

%s' % (n, f, old))

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The standard and the sources

POSITIONS.md:25
- P-25 **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished 2012 restart (F-166) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, it is their latest intent, which the goal is to finish. It covers the exclusion rule, as instantiation exclusion in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, and `Bottom`, which no program can write.

POSITIONS.md:28
- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Next is the algebraic layer: `Ring`, `Field` and what the matrices and tensors of machine learning need, so that the library's traits reach them. It goes into the standard library itself (P-27), not into a tree of the revival's own.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:36
- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library the compiler checks.** The interpreter's `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin` become the compiled path's library. He sees the compiler's prelude (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`) as a bootstrap to remove, so no declaration goes into it, and its three files are deleted at the switch-over with their tests kept. Code-generator rungs go on. How the checker comes to accept the library is a plan shown to him step by step, not a question to ask again. Still to build: PLAN phase 4.

POSITIONS.md:38
- P-39 **The checker count is measured in every gate and never turns the gate red.** The gate reports the count stage on its own. The distance to the switch-over (F-53), over all apis and components, is a report-only stage of the phase-3 gates, whose work drives it down.

POSITIONS.md:54
- P-55 **A size may hold arithmetic, compared by its written form once numerals are folded (item 15, 15a with (b)).** The checker accepts a sum, difference, product or power in a size. `2 3` folds to `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. The class loader computes the value when it makes a class. A size name may equal a numeral, as the team's Q&A answers, so the `N[\0\]` arm of a `typecase N[\b0\]` is reachable. The library keeps the team's sizes written as products and sums. Two later array forks stand at defaults while his answers are pending: fork 3, a size known only at run time, at way 4a, where his reading of P-40 is asked; and fork 2, the bound of `Vector` and `Matrix`, at the two-trait bound (PLAN items 13 and 52).

POSITIONS.md:44
- P-45 **Overloads may differ in their static parameters (answer 9).** The specification drops its sentence that forbids it and states the type group's 2011 model, which the checker runs; the old sentence stays as superseded text. The checker keeps the paper's three overloading rules, checks the Return Type Rule over every instance, and requires two generic declarations in the more-specific relation to agree on their static parameters position by position, as Java's overriding rule does (row 398). Walk dispatches on declared domains, not by the order of the declarations, and its load check reads every pair of generic declarations on their declared domains by the checker's rules, with no parameter pair required to exclude, so that walk and the checker accept the same pairs (row 159). The library repairs its refused families with its own exclusions, and no model line changes. The judgement's smaller choices took the record's defaults, listed for his review in `PLAN.md`. Built: walk's load check over every pair of functions with static parameters, by climb batch 17's rung G. Not built: a functional method of a generic trait or object is still compared on its instances (F-26), the Meet Rule's search matches only some domains (row 539), two nested generic functional methods of a trait or object are refused at load where the same two functions load (row 779), and in a trait with static parameters load and fail at a call (row 780). Rung G's reading makes walk and the checker disagree on row 759's pair: walk refuses `g[\T\](a: T)` beside `g(a: Any)`, and the checker accepts it. Climb batch 19's reading of exclusion (P-152) leaves three more, rows 786 to 788.

POSITIONS.md:63
- P-148 **The checker's speed comes right after its correctness.** A rung that changes the checker measures how the change affects the time that the checker needs. First the rung makes the change correct. Then it does a second pass that makes the checker faster. This pass must not change the checker's results: the checker accepts and refuses the same programs as before, with the same errors at the same places. The rung's skeptic checks the time and the results. This work is part of the rung, not a separate step after the landing. Built in the `fortress-repo` skill (`compiler.md`), the batch script's rung and skeptic prompts, and the batch manual.

The full check programs run only when asked. A slower check is to him a waste of time.

## 6. Measurements

**The setup.** Every run used a fresh private caches folder and `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, from the main tree's build. The command, for each `DIR` and `P`:

```
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
export FORTRESS_HOME=/home/user/fortress FORTRESS_THREADS=1; unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
C=$DIR/run-XXXX/caches; T=$DIR/run-XXXX/tmp; printf '\0\0\0\0' > $C/global.map
export TMPDIR=$T FORTRESS_CACHES=$C JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$T"
cd $DIR && nice -n 19 timeout -k 10 900 $FORTRESS_HOME/bin/fortress [typecheck] P.fss
```

- The machine: nproc 4, Intel Xeon Processor @ 2.10GHz, OpenJDK 25.0.4.1, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`. The loads at start, 8.2 to 19.7, came from climb batch 19's run, so no timing below is a measure.
- The probe programs were scratch and are not kept. Their declarations are quoted below.
- Three earlier runs of M1 stopped at load on slips of mine, and are not results:
  - a parameter named `label`, a keyword;
  - `PrimitiveArray` and `N` without `import NativeArray.{...}` and `import NatReflect.{...}`;
  - `Ratio`, which the api does not export, so the `QQ` case was dropped.

**M1, `ProbeLeafWays.fss` under walk** (load at start 15.78; rc=0, 28 s).

- The declarations:
  - `trait LeafVec[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat s0\] extends { Array1[\T,0,s0\] }` redeclares `tabulate(f:ZZ32->T): LeafVec[\T,s0\]` and `fill(v:T): LeafVec[\T,s0\]` with `StandardMutableArrayType`'s bodies, and `plusT` built through `tabulate`;
  - `object LeafStore` holds a `PrimitiveArray`, with `replica` `array1`;
  - `plusCast(a,b) = cast[\Vector[\T,s0\]\](a.ivmap[\T\](fn (i, e) => e + b.get(i)))`, `negCast` through `map`, `mPlusCast` through `Matrix`'s `ivmap`, `fillCast`;
  - `bf1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]()`: `__builtinFactory1`'s body with `N[\0\] => cast[\Array1[\T,b0,s0\]\](r)`;
  - the column subscript `a[(0,1)#(2,1)]` of a 2 × 3 `ZZ32` array.
- The output:

```

1a fill answers the leaf type: yes
1b tabulate-built body answers the leaf type: yes
1c RR64 plus [0#3][ 0.0 1.0 2.0 ] neg [0#3][ -0.0 -0.5 -1.0 ]
1c ZZ32 plus [0#3][ 0 2 4 ] neg [0#3][ 0 -1 -2 ]
1c NN32 plus [0#3][ 0 2 4 ]
1c RR32 plus [0#2][ 3.0 3.0 ]
1c TransposedMatrix plus [0#3,0#2]
1c the parent's map on a transposed matrix is a Matrix: yes
2a arm at b0 = 0 gives a Vector: yes
2a arm at b0 = 2 gives an Array1 based at 2: yes
3d the column subscript's value is a sized rank-2 array of 2 by 1: yes
3d cast column 1 11 and the library's a[:,1] 1 11
```

**M2, `ProbeDeadSizes.fss` under walk** (load at start 9.21; rc=0, 30 s).

- The declarations: `dot1[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat n, nat m, nat p\](me: Vector[\T,n\], other: Vector[\T,n\]): T = me.dot(other)`, and the api's pair `dotD` (vector and scalar), both with the dead `m` and `p`. Each is called without static arguments.
- The output: `dot1 14.0`, `dotD vector 14.0`, `dotD scalar [0#3][ 2.0 4.0 6.0 ]`.

**M3, `ProbeCover2` through `fortress typecheck`** (load at start 19.68; rc=255, 9 s).

- The api declares `h(): ZZ32`, which the component lacks, and `f[\T, nat s0, nat s1, nat s2\](): ZZ32`. The component defines `f()` and `f(v: T)`.
- The output reports `h` alone:

```
Component ProbeCover2 exports API ProbeCover2
but does not define all declarations in ProbeCover2.
Missing declarations: {h():ZZ32 at …/ProbeCover2.fsi:4:1-6:64}
```

**M4, `ProbeCover` and M5, `ProbeCover3`, through `fortress typecheck`.** rc=0, no error, 13 s and 11 s.

- M4: the api declares `f[\T\](): ZZ32` alone and `g` in both forms; the component defines both forms of each.
- M5: the same shape with a sized generic result, `f[\T, nat s0\](): Box3[\T,0,s0\]` alone in the api, beside `f(v: T)` in the component.

## 7. Found on the way

- **The export check is stricter than `apis.tex` in two places** (my reading of `ExportChecker.scala:766-805` against `apis.tex:249-256` and the text it quotes at `:327-339`):
  - it refuses a concrete component member for an api's `abstract` one: `Equality`'s `=`, `Indexed`'s `size`;
  - it counts the api's abstract members as required.

# Made from plan-18/manifest/gen18.py for climb batch 19; it reads the same fields, "lands only with" among them.
# Generates climb batch 19's MANIFEST block (CLIMB-BATCH-19.md, rungs P and S) for the batch workflow
# (explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js; explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/batch-redesign.md)
# from the record and the briefings of lists19.py, into $OUT19/manifest19.js ($FORTRESS_HOME/tmp by default, which
# is ignored); check19.js checks it and splices it. On batch 15's pattern (plan-15/manifest/gen15.py): each rung's
# section of the record's section 3 goes into the block word for word as the rung's section, which every role on the
# rung reads (the worker, the skeptic, a judge and a repair round), its code-span backticks dropped and any ellipsis
# character written as three full stops, since the script carries ASCII only; the briefing's reasons go beside the
# keys, and the script renders them at the end of the worker's brief; the manifest fields (slug, worktree, expected
# minutes, the stage as the test, the step a rung brings into the gate, the checker count a rung declares, the rungs
# it lands only with, the blurb and the points to report) come from the record's section 5, "The manifest, rung by
# rung", and the intro every agent reads from its "What every agent of the run reads first". No value is set at
# launch: the gather numbers the batch's new rows through ledger.py, so the block has no LEDGER_FROM. No rung
# declares a checker count, and none lands only with another.
#   python3 -B gen19.py [RECORD]      RECORD defaults to explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-19.md
import json, re, sys, os
HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
sys.path.insert(0, HERE)
from lists19 import LISTS, REASONS, IDS

ROOT = os.environ.get('FORTRESS_HOME', os.path.abspath(os.path.join(HERE, '../../../..')))
args = [a for a in sys.argv[1:] if not a.startswith('--')]
REC = args[0] if args else os.path.join(ROOT, 'explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-19.md')
OUT = os.path.join(os.environ.get('OUT19', os.path.join(ROOT, 'tmp')), 'manifest19.js')
os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(OUT), exist_ok=True)
rec = open(REC, encoding='utf-8').read()


def ascii_text(t):
    t = t.replace('`', '').replace('…', '...')
    bad = [c for c in t if ord(c) > 127]
    assert not bad, ('non-ASCII left', bad, t[:120])
    return t


def between(text, start, end):
    i = text.index(start)
    j = text.index(end, i + len(start))
    return text[i + len(start):j]


# Section 3: one block per rung, from its heading to the next ### heading.
s3 = between(rec, '\n## 3. The rungs\n', '\n## 4. ')
heads = list(re.finditer(r'^### ([A-Z])\. (.*)$', s3, flags=re.M))
assert [h.group(1) for h in heads] == list(IDS), [h.group(1) for h in heads]
sections, titles = {}, {}
for i, h in enumerate(heads):
    rid = h.group(1)
    end = heads[i + 1].start() if i + 1 < len(heads) else s3.index('\n### The rule the rungs keep')
    body = s3[h.end():end].strip('\n')
    assert body.startswith('**The answers this rung follows.**'), rid
    sections[rid] = ascii_text(body)
    titles[rid] = ascii_text(h.group(2))

# Section 5: the manifest fields, rung by rung, and the intro.
s5 = rec[rec.index('\n## 5. How it is run\n'):]
mrung = between(s5, '\n### The manifest, rung by rung\n', '\n### What every agent of the run reads first\n')
blocks = list(re.finditer(r'^#### ([A-Z])$', mrung, flags=re.M))
assert [b.group(1) for b in blocks] == list(IDS), [b.group(1) for b in blocks]
FIELDS = {}
for i, b in enumerate(blocks):
    rid = b.group(1)
    text = mrung[b.end():blocks[i + 1].start() if i + 1 < len(blocks) else len(mrung)]
    f, points, in_points = {}, [], False
    for line in text.split('\n'):
        m = re.match(r'^- \*\*([a-z ]+):\*\*\s*(.*)$', line)
        if m:
            key, val = m.group(1), m.group(2).strip()
            in_points = (key == 'points to report')
            if not in_points:
                f[key] = ascii_text(val)
            continue
        m = re.match(r'^  - (.*)$', line)
        if m and in_points:
            points.append(ascii_text(m.group(1).strip()))
    f['points'] = points
    for k in ('slug', 'worktree', 'expected minutes', 'its test is the stage', 'writes state', 'joins the gate', 'checker count', 'lands only with', 'blurb'):
        assert k in f, (rid, k)
    assert points, (rid, 'no points to report')
    FIELDS[rid] = f
intro = between(s5, '\n### What every agent of the run reads first\n', '\n### Before the launch\n').strip()

A('// ===========================================================================')
A('')
A("const BATCH = '19'")
A("const BATCH_RECORD = 'explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-19.md'")
A("const BRIEFING_LISTS = 'explorations/compile-ladder/plan-19/manifest/lists19.py'")
A('')
for rid in IDS:
    A('const %s_SECTION = [' % rid)
    for l in sections[rid].split('\n'):
        A(js(l) + ',')
    A("].join('\\n')")
    A('')
for rid in IDS:

    slug = f['slug']

    joins = [] if f['joins the gate'] == 'none' else [x.strip() for x in f['joins the gate'].split(',')]
    A("const %s_ENTRY = { id: '%s', slug: '%s', path: '%s', branch: 'wip/%s', expectedMinutes: %d," % (rid, rid, slug, path, slug, int(f['expected minutes'])))
    cc = f['checker count']

    A('    writesState: %s, testIsStage: %s, gateJoins: %s, expectedMoves: [],%s%s' % ('true' if yes(f['writes state']) else 'false', 'true' if yes(f['its test is the stage']) else 'false', js(joins), '' if cc == 'none' else ' expectedCheckerCount: %d,' % int(cc), '' if not lw else ' landsOnlyWith: %s,' % js(lw)))
    A('    title: ' + js(titles[rid]) + ',')

def reason_problems(rid):
    out = []
    for k, r in REASONS[rid]:
        if not r or not r.strip():
            out.append((k, 'no reason'))
        elif '\n' in r or '`' in r or any(ord(c) > 127 for c in r):
            out.append((k, 'a reason is one ASCII line with no backtick'))
        elif not r.endswith('.') or len(r) > 240:
            out.append((k, 'a reason ends with a full stop and is at most 240 characters'))
    return out

            print(rid, name, 'keys', len(keys), 'exit', r.returncode, '|', total[0] if total else r.stderr.strip()[:200])

            if r.returncode or probs:

                if os.environ.get('VERBOSE'): print(r.stdout)
    print('bad lists', bad)
    sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)
